brief.head: Weaken, wrap or build
brief.text: Vaccines are made by weak­en­ing a pathogen, by hid­ing its spike in a harm­less car­rier, or by build­ing a looka­like mol­e­cule, Ajay Shah said. mRNA be­longs to the last. {027-C09}

brief.head: America’s gift
brief.text: The US FDA is too con­ser­va­tive and slow, Ajay Shah said, but its pub­lished test­ing is a global pub­lic good. India should im­port from global man­u­fac­tur­ers. {027-C11}

brief.head: Cheap, and nowhere
brief.text: Price caps meant to help the poor dis­cour­age pro­duc­ers and al­ways cre­ate scarcity, Amit Varma said. A cheap vac­cine you can­not find does you no good. {027-C07}

brief.head: Drowsier than drunk
brief.text: From Matthew Walker’s *Why We Sleep*, Amit Varma learnt that driv­ers short of sleep cause more ac­ci­dents than drunk ones. Drunk driv­ing is dan­ger­ous; sleepy driv­ing more so. {027-R01}

brief.head: Influenza, misheard
brief.text: Ajay Shah once told Amit Varma to take the in­fluenza vac­cine. Varma heard “in­flu­encer”, and signed up at once: “You had me at hello.” {027-J02}

thought.label: Thought for the day
thought.text: A vac­cine is first and fore­most a pri­vate good.
thought.who: Ajay Shah, starting the case for vaccines from freedom rather than the state

lead.kicker: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah on vaccines and the state
lead.head: Love the jab, question the strap

pic.caption: Ajay Shah (left) and Amit Varma early in Episode 27

body: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah are fans of vac­cines. They are also fans of free­dom. In India, Varma said, that is where things get “a lit­tle messy and com­pli­cated”.
Shah called the ex­er­cise “the tool­kit in ac­tion”: the frame­work from their two pre­vi­ous episodes, on the state and on when it should act, ap­plied to one ques­tion. {#toolkit}
First came the gush­ing. Something is in­jected into your body, per­haps in two or three shots, Shah said, and a dis­ease is gone from your life. “Is this mag­i­cal or what?”
He traced the story from pus-smeared in­oc­u­la­tion through Edward Jenner’s cow­pox to a Covid vac­cine de­signed by soft­ware.
## Freedom first
Then Varma read out the pop­u­lar case for the state: fund re­search, run the fac­to­ries, ban im­ports, plan every jab and force the un­will­ing. “I think they’re all rub­bish,” he said.
Shah an­swered from first prin­ci­ples. Freedom is the de­fault, so begin with no state at all and ask what, if any­thing, fails.
“A vac­cine is first and fore­most a pri­vate good,” he said. The per­son who gets it ben­e­fits most, as with eat­ing a choco­late or get­ting a toothache fixed. {027-C01}

There is a mar­ket fail­ure: your vac­ci­na­tion also pro­tects the peo­ple around you, a pos­i­tive ex­ter­nal­ity. But it bites only for those who will not pay. Anyone who buys a vac­cine out of self-interest is done.

Unlike ed­u­ca­tion, where ev­ery­one un­der­in­vests, a vac­cine is a yes-or-no de­ci­sion. “Vaccines are only in­te­ger val­ued,” Shah said. “They’re the zero or they’re one. For the ones, it’s game over.” {027-C03}
For the zeros, the an­swer is a voucher: the state tops up what a per­son would pay. That jus­ti­fies fund­ing, Shah said, not state fac­to­ries, im­port bans or cen­tral plan­ning.
## The strap ques­tion

Eradication is dif­fer­ent. The com­mon cold moves among many species, in­clud­ing pigs, and ra­bies sur­vives in dogs and foxes. But small­pox and polio live only in hu­mans, so they can be wiped out.
A world with­out small­pox, Shah ar­gued, is a true pub­lic good: nobody’s share of it di­min­ishes any­one else’s, and no new­born can be shut out. {027-C04}
That raised a moral puz­zle. A state that touches your body, Shah said, ranks with the death penalty, tor­ture and in­car­cer­a­tion in in­tru­sive­ness. What of con­sci­en­tious ob­jec­tors?

For erad­i­ca­tion alone, Shah would sign up for sig­nif­i­cant co­er­cion, though each lis­tener must de­cide. Varma, cast as the man strapped down, protested: “You re­ally want to strap me down, don’t you?”
Varma set his own bar. The co­er­cion he cheers today, he ar­gued, could to­mor­row be used for some­thing he op­poses. Where forc­ing hap­pens, “the bar should be very high.” {027-C06}
Shah added a darker thought: fu­ture biotech­nol­ogy might give gov­ern­ments vac­cines that “make a pop­u­la­tion more docile, more con­trol­lable”.
## Roll up your sleeve

The episode closed with a pre­scrip­tion. Shah wants vac­cines counted among ev­ery­day health-seeking be­hav­iours, with sleep hy­giene, nu­tri­tion and ex­er­cise, and adults to take the whole array made for them.
“Vaccines are not a zone of gov­ern­ment,” he said. “They should be a zone of the peo­ple.” Post them on Instagram, he urged, and give your friends FOMO.
Varma, who got Covishield the very day he could, promised to take many of the vac­cines Shah rec­om­mends.

body: When Covid broke out, Amit Varma re­called, some ex­perts pre­dicted we might never find a vac­cine. {#never} Vaccines had tra­di­tion­ally taken years, if not decades, and the search for an HIV vac­cine still goes on.
Instead, Ajay Shah said, “some folks in China se­quenced the SARS-CoV-2 and up­loaded a file. Then a piece of soft­ware read that file and printed out the de­sign of the mRNA vac­cine.” {027-S03}

All the re­main­ing delay, Shah said, came from test­ing by the US FDA and from build­ing fac­to­ries to scale up. The de­sign it­self, Varma noted, came prac­ti­cally the same day the virus was se­quenced and put on­line.

third.head: How the wheels came off

pic.caption: Ajay Shah on the show’s name

body: Before the show, a short­list. Amit Varma said the hosts brain­stormed for a long time, not about con­tent but about a name. Two made the final: *Watching the Wheels* and *Everything is Everything*.
The first is John Lennon’s song, which Ajay Shah called con­tem­pla­tive and hum­ble: the uni­verse trun­dles along while we watch “with an air of amuse­ment”. {#lennon} Everyone would know it.

The sec­ond is a line from Bruce Springsteen’s *You’re Missing*, on *The Rising*, the album he wrote after the 9/11 at­tacks. Shah said: “So it’s like my world is here, ev­ery­thing is there, but you are miss­ing.” {027-S05}
Tested on many peo­ple, the sec­ond won. Lennon still opens the episode: the hosts’ young friend Ishaan Chintamani sang *Watching the Wheels* for them, with his fa­ther Gaurav on gui­tar. {#ishaan}

p2.title: Needles and liberty
p2.deck: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah put their framework for state action to work on vaccines {#toolkit}

from1.head: Love the jab, question the strap

quote.text: mRNA is ab­so­lutely mag­i­cal. It’s a mir­a­cle of mod­ern sci­ence. It’s one of the great­est achieve­ments.

box.title: Two episodes before this one
box.text: Episodes 25 and 26, *Understanding the State* and *When Should the State Act?*, built a gen­eral method for pub­lic pol­icy: free­dom is the de­fault, so hunt first for mar­ket fail­ures. This episode, Ajay Shah said, is a demo of it. {#demo}

sections.label: The marvel
sections.head: Better than the moon
sections.caption: the miracle of vaccines
body: “I love vac­cines,” Ajay Shah said. “Vaccines are the great­est thing. It’s like as cool as going to the moon and back.” {#moon}
Shah said he is grate­ful to the uni­verse for hav­ing made so many vac­cines, to match all the pathogens Mother Nature left wan­der­ing around the planet try­ing to get their teeth into us.
Their an­ces­tors were crude. Inoculators smeared small­pox pus into cuts; Edward Jenner found that cow­pox pro­tected with­out killing. Modern vac­cines, Shah said, come in three kinds.
## Three recipes
Attenuated vac­cines take a pure cul­ture of the pathogen and dam­age it, with heat, acid or other tech­niques, leav­ing enough for the im­mune sys­tem to learn from.

Engineered car­ri­ers are the sec­ond route. The AstraZeneca vac­cine, sold in India as Covishield, places the SARS-CoV-2 spike in­side a chim­panzee virus harm­less to hu­mans, and in­jects some­thing like a tril­lion par­ti­cles. {#trillion} The im­mune sys­tem learns the pro­tein sur­face of the spike, so the body is ready when the real virus shows up.

Synthetic vac­cines con­struct a novel mol­e­cule that looks like the virus, and mRNA be­longs here. Shah said he was not the right per­son to ex­plain it, but called it “a pin­na­cle of human knowl­edge of bi­ol­ogy”.

~ A man­u­fac­tured vac­cine car­ries no risk of get­ting sick, he said, whereas some at­ten­u­ated vac­cines make one per­son in ten thou­sand ill. Very high ef­fi­cacy, often near-zero side ef­fects: to Shah, all of it is a mir­a­cle. {027-C09}

quote.text: mRNA is ab­so­lutely mag­i­cal. It’s a mir­a­cle of mod­ern sci­ence. It’s one of the great­est achieve­ments.

sections.label: The first test
sections.head: Zero, one, game over
sections.caption: vaccines as a private good
body: Amit Varma listed the pop­u­lar wis­dom: the state should fund re­search, run fac­to­ries, ban im­ports, plan every jab and co­erce re­fusers. Whisper “com­mit­tee, bud­get” in a bureaucrat’s ear at bed­time, he said, and “they’ll go to sleep with a be­atific smile on their face”. {027-J01}
Ajay Shah began where the tool­kit be­gins. Freedom is the de­fault: imag­ine no state at all, then ask what, if any­thing, fails.

The an­swer starts with self-interest. Get vac­ci­nated and you are pro­tected, as surely as you get util­ity from a choco­late. “A vac­cine is first and fore­most a pri­vate good,” Shah said. {027-C01}

The mar­ket fail­ure is a pos­i­tive ex­ter­nal­ity. In a stu­dio where Shah gabs “at high speed”, his vac­ci­na­tion pro­tects Varma too. But it mat­ters only for those who de­cline to pay. {027-C02}
## Taken or not
That sets vac­cines apart from ed­u­ca­tion, where every sin­gle per­son un­der­in­vests, so the fail­ure is uni­ver­sal. A vac­cine is taken or not taken. “For the ones, it’s game over.” {027-C03}
For the zeros, the stan­dard fix is a voucher: the state tops up a person’s own will­ing­ness to pay, to re­flect the gain to ev­ery­one else.

~ For a fright­en­ing enough dis­ease, peo­ple will buy vac­cines un­prompted; for flu there are shades of grey. Either way, Shah said, an ex­ter­nal­ity mo­ti­vates fund­ing, not the rest of Varma’s list.

quote.text: Then ac­tu­ally, for me, the story is over, there is no mar­ket fail­ure.

sections.label: The high bar
sections.head: Wiped out, and good for all
sections.caption: eradication and the body
body: Some dis­eases can never be beaten. The com­mon cold moves in and out of many species, in­clud­ing pigs, Ajay Shah said, and ra­bies has a reser­voir in dogs and foxes. You sim­ply make do.
A few pathogens, such as small­pox and polio, live only in hu­mans. Get the vac­cine to every per­son in the world and the hor­ror is gone for­ever.

Such a world, Shah ar­gued, is a pub­lic good. The show’s young cam­era crew, Vaishnav and Nomsita, never had a small­pox vac­cine; only “old peo­ple like me” had. No one’s en­joy­ment of a small­pox-free world di­min­ishes another’s, and no new­born can be ex­cluded. {027-C04}
## Hands off the body
Then came the puz­zle. A state that touches your body, Shah said, sits with the death penalty, tor­ture and in­car­cer­a­tion on the scale of in­tru­sion. {027-C05}

What of a few thou­sand con­sci­en­tious ob­jec­tors who refuse a small­pox vac­cine on re­li­gious grounds? Shah pic­tured of­fi­cials strap­ping down “Amit Bhai” as he hollered and screamed, “a scene straight out of *One Flew Over the Cuckoo’s Nest*”. Varma asked which Amit Bhai he meant. {027-J04}

~ Shah’s an­swer: for small­pox or polio erad­i­ca­tion, he would sign on for sig­nif­i­cant co­er­cion. But he called him­self “a tiny ir­rel­e­vant per­son”. Each of us, he said, must make our own choice.

quote.text: Eradication projects and only erad­i­ca­tion projects have the high bar of pub­lic goods.

art.caption: Ajay Shah on eradication and the body

sections.label: The principle
sections.head: Coercion, the other epidemic
sections.caption: consent and coercion
body: Amit Varma calls him­self “a huge pro vac­cine” per­son; he got vac­ci­nated against Covid the very day it was pos­si­ble. {#covishield} He is also, he said, “a huge pro free­dom per­son”, and to him con­sent mat­ters.

Should a good thing be forced on peo­ple? The co­er­cion he favours today, Varma ar­gued, might to­mor­row be used for some­thing he op­poses. The ques­tion is whether the forc­ing it­self is good, and the bar should be very high. {027-C06}
Coercion, he said, is a so­cial ill, and “a more en­demic dis­ease than any other”.
Ajay Shah of­fered a rea­son for cau­tion. Future bi­o­log­i­cal tech­nol­ogy, he said, might let gov­ern­ments use vac­cines “that make a pop­u­la­tion more docile, more con­trol­lable”. {#docile}
## Cloaked in kind­ness
Varma named two co­er­cions with good in­ten­tions and bad out­comes. The first is price con­trols, which dis­cour­age pro­duc­ers and in­no­va­tors and hurt the poor more than they help. {027-C07}

The sec­ond is a state mo­nop­oly on sup­ply, which only slows vac­ci­na­tion. Let the gov­ern­ment run its pro­gramme, Varma said, but let pri­vate play­ers in too. When richer peo­ple pay “a bomb” for an mRNA vac­cine, scarce cheap sup­ply is freed for those who can­not af­ford it. {027-C08}
~ Shah’s only doubt was about the good in­ten­tions. “I’m not even sure about the in­ten­tions,” he said.

quote.text: And price con­trols al­ways lead to scarci­ties. All it means is you won’t get the damn thing.

art.caption: Ajay Shah on consent and coercion

sections.label: The prescription
sections.head: Show off your shots
sections.caption: adult vaccines
body: Amit Varma de­scribed him­self as “like a lit­tle boy bub­bling with joy”. Tell him choco­lates are good, and he wants choco­lates. Tell him vac­cines are good: “I want vac­cines.”

Ajay Shah wants vac­cines en­shrined as a first-class part of health-seeking be­hav­iour, along­side sleep hy­giene, nu­tri­tion and ex­er­cise. Many of us think vac­cines are for chil­dren, or are some­thing the gov­ern­ment does. Both propo­si­tions, he said, are wrong.
“Vaccines are not a zone of gov­ern­ment,” he said. “They should be a zone of the peo­ple.” Tell your friends you fin­ished your third dose. Put the pic­ture on Instagram. Create FOMO. {027-C10}
## A free lunch

Shah pointed read­ers to the US CDC’s list of adult vac­cines, ap­proved by the US FDA, and its sched­ule by age, show­ing which need a new shot every year or every three years. The list runs to 18 vac­cines. {#eighteen}

He thinks the FDA too con­ser­va­tive and too slow. That makes its ap­proval a high bar, and its pub­lished test­ing a global pub­lic good. India and Bangladesh, he said, should im­port from global man­u­fac­tur­ers. {027-C11}
The hosts’ friend Rajeshwari Sengupta paid for 42 vac­cines for her child. {#fortytwo}
~ Paying up front to rule out dis­ease is, to Shah, “just a free lunch”. Prevention is bet­ter than cure.

quote.text: So some­thing being ap­proved by the US FDA is a high bar.
But to­mor­row it might be some­thing I’m not in favour of, which is being forced upon me. So we should go to the prin­ci­ple it­self. Is the forc­ing good? Is the forc­ing bad?

p3.title: Tales of the pox
p3.deck: Pus, cows, a guru’s dream and a city that falls ill

stories.kicker: Ajay Shah on a hippie, a guru and India’s smallpox fight
stories.head: Sent down the hill by a goddess
body: In the early 1970s, Ajay Shah said, small­pox had been erad­i­cated through most of the world. India, Nepal, Bangladesh, Ethiopia and Somalia were the last hold­outs, a reser­voir from which the dis­ease could one day bounce back. {#holdouts}

Among the colour­ful char­ac­ters in the fight was Larry Brilliant, a hip­pie liv­ing with a Hindu spir­i­tual guide in the Himalayas. Shah for­got the guru’s name; Amit Varma sup­plied it: Neem Karoli Baba.
One day the Baba said a god­dess had told him in a dream that Larry must go down to the plains and con­quer small­pox. Larry was baf­fled: what could he do? The Baba or­dered him out.

Larry left the ashram near Rishikesh and took the overnight bus. At 4 a.m. he reached the WHO com­pound in Delhi. {#fouram} Nobody was there; some dogs were bark­ing. With nowhere else to go, he slept at the gate.

In the morn­ing, peo­ple came and won­dered who he was. He had a de­gree in medicine, so they signed him on as a ju­nior flunky in the small­pox pro­gramme. “He was bril­liant,” Shah said. “He was very bril­liant.” {027-J05}
One thing led to an­other, and Larry Brilliant ended up as one of the top peo­ple who led India’s small­pox erad­i­ca­tion pro­gramme. {027-S04}
~ Varma, for his part, had an­other the­ory about the dream: per­haps Larry had not bathed for three days, and the Baba made up the god­dess to be rid of him. “Enough is enough,” said Shah. {027-J06}
stories.why: One of the great pub­lic-health tri­umphs in India turned partly on chance: a guru’s dream, an overnight bus and a hip­pie asleep at a gate. Small, odd events, the story shows, can have vast con­se­quences for the world.
stories.postscript: Shah loves the small­pox story so much, he said, that he could not re­sist telling it: “a tri­umph of human achieve­ment”.

pic.caption: Ajay Shah on Larry Brilliant and the goddess’s dream

stories.kicker: Ajay Shah on the gruesome ancestor of the vaccine
stories.head: A little pus, a lot of nerve
body: Smallpox killed a quar­ter of the chil­dren who caught it, Ajay Shah said, and over the first ten or twenty years of life al­most ev­ery­one met it. {#quarter}

The an­swer was mild ex­po­sure. Inoculators broke a pus­tule on an in­fected per­son, cut a healthy child’s skin and smeared in the white pus. “Does that sound suit­ably dis­gust­ing and gross and scary as hell?” Shah asked. {027-S01}

About one in ten in­oc­u­lated chil­dren still caught small­pox and died. But 10 per cent beats 25. Shah said there is fair ev­i­dence the prac­tice began in India, though per­haps in the Ottoman Empire; it likely trav­elled on to Europe’s im­pe­rial courts.
~ The trou­ble was the dose. Smallpox is so vir­u­lent, Shah said, that a tenth or a hun­dredth as much pus prob­a­bly made lit­tle dif­fer­ence to the risk. {#dose}
stories.why: People un­der­stood the prin­ci­ple of im­mu­nity long be­fore they un­der­stood the bi­ol­ogy. Without a way to con­trol the dose, though, pro­tec­tion came at a ter­ri­ble price, and the next leap would be keep­ing the pro­tec­tion with­out the killing.

stories.kicker: Ajay Shah on the relative that protected against smallpox
stories.head: Cowpox to the rescue
body: Edward Jenner no­ticed that the women who worked with cows often caught cow­pox, a rel­a­tive of small­pox. Once they had it, Ajay Shah said, they were com­pletely im­mu­nised against small­pox.
This was se­ri­ously great, Shah said, be­cause cow­pox does not kill at a 10 per cent prob­a­bil­ity, as in­oc­u­la­tion did. It is a minor dis­ease. {#cowpox}
The trick lay in the gap. Cowpox is dif­fer­ent enough from small­pox not to kill you, and close enough to de­liver pro­tec­tion. It was, Shah said, a huge leap in think­ing. {027-S02}

~ Inoculators al­ready knew that ex­po­sure pro­tects. Jenner’s idea, Shah said, was pro­tec­tion “with­out killing a large frac­tion of the peo­ple”, and from it grew the whole mod­ern idea of vac­cines.

quote.text: That was a huge in­tel­lec­tual break­through by Edward Jenner.

pic.caption: Ajay Shah on Edward Jenner and cowpox

stories.kicker: Amit Varma on a surreal novel he never wrote
stories.head: The city that caught smallpox
body: In his early twen­ties, Amit Varma read a great book on small­pox, whose name he has for­got­ten, and a de­tailed *New Yorker* essay.
They gave him an idea for a novel called *Smallpox Town*, writ­ten as one word. “And in that a city get small­pox. Not the peo­ple in the city. The city gets small­pox.” {027-S06}

The build­ings would break out in pus­tules and the ground would scab over. Whatever hap­pens in the course of the dis­ease would hap­pen not to the peo­ple but to the city: “suf­fi­ciently dystopian and sur­real”, he said.

~ He was young, and for­got the idea, until Ajay Shah’s small­pox story brought it back. He con­fessed he had not read Albert Camus’s *The Plague*, though he had read *L’Etranger*, and re­cited its open­ing: “my mother died today, or was it yes­ter­day”. {027-J11}
stories.why: Reading non-fiction about a dis­ease can spark sur­real fic­tion. And an idea for­got­ten since one’s early twen­ties can resur­face years later, when a friend’s story about the same dis­ease touches the right nerve.

quiz.q: What did early inoculators smear into a cut on a healthy child’s skin?
quiz.a: White pus from a bro­ken pus­tule on some­one sick with small­pox.

quiz.q: Why did women who worked with cows escape smallpox, as Edward Jenner noticed?
quiz.a: They caught cow­pox, a mild rel­a­tive, which left them im­mune to small­pox.

quiz.q: Why does Ajay Shah call vaccines ‘integer valued’, unlike spending on education?
quiz.a: You take it or you don’t, and for tak­ers there is no mar­ket fail­ure.

quiz.q: Why can smallpox and polio be eradicated, but never rabies or the common cold?
quiz.a: Smallpox and polio live only in hu­mans; the oth­ers have an­i­mal reser­voirs.

quiz.q: Who ordered Larry Brilliant down to the plains to fight smallpox, and why?
quiz.a: Neem Karoli Baba, who said a god­dess had told him so in a dream.

quiz.q: What did Amit Varma learn about drivers from Matthew Walker’s *Why We Sleep*?
quiz.a: Drivers short of sleep cause more ac­ci­dents than driv­ers who are drunk.

p4.credits: Everything is Everything was Amit Varma and Ajay Shah’s weekly show, 128 episodes from June 2023 to December 2025. This edition is made from Episode 27. The moving pictures, stills and chapter cards are from its video; the chapter art is by Simahina. Every play button starts the video at the moment it was said. The articles and headlines were written by Claude, an AI model, from the episode’s machine-made transcript, and checked against it. Other photographs are from Wikimedia Commons: COVID-19 vaccine (Administración del Principado de Asturias, CC BY-SA 4.0); Albert Camus (graph by United Press International, public domain); Bruce Springsteen (Raph_PH, CC BY 4.0). The covers on the shelf are from Amazon, Apple and Open Library.

shelf.title: Why We Sleep
shelf.creator: Matthew Walker
shelf.why: The book that taught Amit how un­der­rated sleep is: with­out it you can’t be your best self, sleep-deprived driv­ers are more dan­ger­ous than drunk ones, and night owls, roughly 30% of peo­ple, sim­ply run on a dif­fer­ent rhythm.

shelf.title: Beggars in Spain (Sleepless series)
shelf.creator: Nancy Kress
shelf.why: He calls it a phe­nom­e­nal sci­ence fic­tion book.

shelf.title: A History of Global Health: Interventions into the Lives of Other Peoples
shelf.creator: Randall M. Packard
shelf.why: It is one of the great books in pub­lic health, a field Ajay says is prac­ti­cally ab­sent in India.

shelf.title: The Economics and Politics of Vaccines (Episode 223 of The Seen and the Unseen)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
shelf.why: Ajay on the eco­nom­ics and pol­i­tics of vac­cines, which Amit calls a pot­ted mas­ter­class on health­care: why pre­ven­tion beats cure, and why pub­lic health and health­care are dif­fer­ent things.

shelf.title: Understanding the State (Episode 25)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
shelf.why: The foun­da­tion of the show’s think­ing on gov­ern­ment: the state is a mo­nop­oly on vi­o­lence that acts through co­er­cion, so every in­ter­ven­tion, paid for by taxes, must be jus­ti­fied.

shelf.title: When Should the State Act? (Episode 26)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
shelf.why: Ajay’s mas­ter­class on mar­ket fail­ure in its pre­cise tech­ni­cal sense (pub­lic goods, ex­ter­nal­i­ties and the rest) and on the nar­row con­di­tions under which the state may in­ter­vene, con­di­tions that are nec­es­sary but not suf­fi­cient.

shelf.title: Watching the Wheels
shelf.creator: John Lennon
shelf.why: A song both hosts love and the run­ner-up name for the pod­cast: con­tem­pla­tive and hum­ble, the uni­verse trundling along while we watch, cu­ri­ous and amused.

shelf.title: Watching the Wheels (Chris Cornell version)
shelf.creator: Chris Cornell
shelf.why: Amit says Chris Cornell’s is his favourite ver­sion of the song.

shelf.title: You’re Missing
shelf.creator: Bruce Springsteen
shelf.why: The Springsteen song that gave the show its name and world­view: its line ‘ev­ery­thing is everything’ points at all the world’s won­ders while mark­ing someone’s ab­sence.

shelf.title: CDC Adult Immunization Schedule (vaccine list and schedule by age)
shelf.creator: US CDC
shelf.why: Ajay calls adult vac­ci­na­tion ‘just a free lunch’: pre­ven­tion is bet­ter than cure.

shelf.title: Price Controls Lead to Shortages and Harm the Poor
shelf.creator: Amit Varma
shelf.why: Amit’s case that you can­not leg­is­late scarcity away: price caps dis­cour­age pro­duc­ers and in­no­va­tors, so goods don’t get cheaper but van­ish into short­ages and black mar­kets, hurt­ing the poor they claim to pro­tect.

shelf.title: Price controls for vaccines?
shelf.creator: Ajay Shah
shelf.why: It ap­plies the episode’s ar­gu­ment against well-meant co­er­cion di­rectly to vac­cine pric­ing dur­ing COVID.

shelf.title: An important change of course by policy in Indian Covid-19 vaccination
shelf.creator: Amrita Agarwal and Ajay Shah
shelf.why: Background read­ing on the Indian COVID vac­cine pol­icy de­bate, which the hosts used as a real-world case of their ar­gu­ment.

shelf.title: How the vaccine story will play out
shelf.creator: Ajay Shah
shelf.why: Further read­ing from Ajay on the eco­nom­ics of COVID vac­cines, writ­ten while the pan­demic was un­fold­ing.

shelf.title: The Outsider (L’Etranger)
shelf.creator: Albert Camus
shelf.why: A Camus novel Amit has read and re­mem­bers well enough to quote.

shelf.title: The Plague
shelf.creator: Albert Camus
shelf.why: Camus’s novel of an epi­demic, of­fered as a nat­u­ral com­pan­ion to a con­ver­sa­tion about dis­ease and imag­i­na­tion.

laughs.text: Amit on the bu­reau­cratic mind: ‘there’s noth­ing as at­trac­tive to a bu­reau­crat as the thought of a gov­ern­ment pro­gram.’ Whisper ‘gov­ern­ment pro­gram, com­mit­tee, budget’ in their ear be­fore bed, and ‘they’ll go to sleep with a be­atific smile on their face and their wife will think they’re hav­ing an af­fair.’

Amit on Ajay’s mum­bling: Ajay once told him to take ‘the in­flu­encer vaccine’. Amit replied: ‘There’s a vac­cine that pro­tects me from in­flu­encers. I’m sign­ing up, give it to me. You had me at hello.’ Ajay had ac­tu­ally said in­fluenza.
After list­ing the pop­u­lar myths about state-run vac­ci­na­tion, Amit says: ‘My blood is al­ready boil­ing. It’s a good time to in­ject me with pus.’

Ajay pic­tures state of­fi­cials ‘strap­ping down Amit Bhai’ as he hollers and screams, ‘a scene straight out of One Flew Over the Cuckoo’s Nest.’ Amit: ‘which Amit Bhai are you talk­ing about? It bet­ter not be me.’ Later Amit adds: ‘You re­ally want to strap me down, don’t you?’
On Larry Brilliant land­ing a job at the WHO: ‘He was bril­liant. He was very bril­liant. He was not just bril­liant, he was very bril­liant.’

Amit’s al­ter­na­tive ex­pla­na­tion for the guru’s dream: per­haps Larry Brilliant hadn’t bathed in three days and Neem Karoli Baba sim­ply made up the god­dess to get rid of him. Ajay: ‘Enough is enough.’

Amit clar­i­fies that ‘adult vaccines’ doesn’t mean ‘vac­cines that have grown up.’ Ajay: ‘Or a vac­cine that makes sure that you’ll never be an adult.’ Amit: ‘That would be an ex­cel­lent vac­cine as well.’
Ajay ex­plains the in­tu­ition be­hind in­oc­u­la­tion with ‘as the old Greek say­ing goes, that which does not de­stroy you makes you stronger.’
Albert Camus’s L’Etranger: Amit re­cites its open­ing, ‘my mother died today, or was it yesterday’, while ad­mit­ting he hasn’t read The Plague.
Tyler Cowen’s ‘self-recommending’: Amit bor­rows it to plug his own Seen and the Unseen episode, adding, ‘but I don’t think he means this.’
